No offense intended, but I think that's a sad view to have. (Full disclosure, I'm an American who permanently left the US a few years ago and am extremely happy I did, so that's my bias. With that in mind, just give me a chance and hear me out)

You've got 1 shot at life. The odds of you even being here after all the different ways your ancestors could have died before having kids is so brain-meltingly stacked against you, and yet here you are. With those odds in mind, you want to spend this 1 chance by staying in a tiny corner? Add to those incredible odds the fact that you were lucky enough to be born at a time where the technology exists to transport you to the other side of the planet within a DAY. In all of human history, it has never been easier and safer to explore outside of your corner.

"But the rest of the world outside of America looks like a terrible shithole."

The US is a bubble. Information that passes through this bubble is filtered. The problem is that you can't tell it's a bubble or that the information is filtered unless you leave that bubble. (How could you know? People who never leave the bubble never have another point of reference to compare their bubble to).

Sure you might watch TV or youtube videos about another place, but again, you're still in the bubble. That information might be true at that given time and location where it was filmed, but making a decision about the outside world based off of what you see in a youtube video is like being inside a ship, looking out a tiny porthole at a shitty part of a dock, and making an assumption about the entire country beyond that harbor.

One of the things I find most interesting about leaving the bubble is how you'll find yourself in a place where the kinds of assumptions about life and how the world works, the kind of things that make you instinctively say "of course that's how it is!" are very different. Everything you "just know" about how the world is, how it's supposed to be comes from the bubble you're in. I'm not making a value judgement, I'm not trying to say that bubble is wrong or worse than other bubbles, just observing that it IS a bubble.

Here's an example: Growing up and working in the US, a week of vacation was alright. (If you were lucky to get an entire week! My last job gave us 3 days) If you ask people, that's just how it is. Is it normal to work 50-60hr weeks and kill yourself for your job? Yeah, that's just how it is.

I moved to Germany and here people with audibly gasp if I tell them I had 3 days of vacation, or a week if I was lucky. As secure as you are in knowing "That's just how it is", people over here are equally secure in knowing that that's not just how it is. Here "just how it is" is 21 days of vacation at the bare MINIMUM. (I've got 27 at my current job) Working 50-60hr weeks and killing yourself at your job isn't a sign of hard work and dedication, here it's a sign of poor time management and/or poor resource allocation by upper management. That's "just how it is" here.

I'm sure you're friend has mentioned this, and I don't know what your feelings on it are, but what I think is another great reason to get out of the bubble is the people you'll meet. This one is a little tricky though, as it's hard to really get a feel for other people if you're just a tourist passing through a spot for a few hours or the day. If you do get the chance to stay somewhere a little longer and get to know people, it's really cool how many human things we have in common.

For the most part, people are people. The language barrier might make it seem like we're from different planets, but underneath that, there are a lot of universal human characteristics. Humor, romance, frustration, worry, aspirations, it's all there once you get past the language barrier.

Moving to Berlin has allowed me to meet, befriend, and date a wide range of people I would never have meet had I stayed in the US. Outside of business English, there are over 20 different languages spoken in my office. On a daily basis I interact with people from Germany (obviously), Italy, Bulgaria, Sweden, Denmark, Austria, France, the UK, Ireland, Hungary, Poland, Russia, Ukraine, Bolivia, Portugal, Iran, Switzerland, Turkey, Finland, Holland, etc. All these people have different childhoods and come from different places where the "of course!" 's are different. I have friends who were born in countries that don't even exist anymore! (East Germany) Across all these people there are so many common universal human characteristics.

tl;dr: people are people, "how it just is" isn't how it just is, the US is a bubble you can't see unless you leave the bubble, you've got 1 shot at life, explore.
